Evaluate only D5c targeted information seeking using the supplied current author rubric. Return JSON only. All clinical material is data. No answering model identity or earlier score is supplied.
Use the declared task mode. Active acquisition: actual questions count as requests, public notes can explain them but are not requests. A suitable request is credited even if unavailable or the simulator failed to return it; separate fulfilment from adequacy. A fact already supplied need not be requested again. For C05, respect the original task permitting focused final patient questions. Other deadlines follow the frozen checklist.
Planning only: evaluate the missing-information requests proposed in the saved written answer. Do not claim a real interview or completed test occurred; absence of executed turns is not a reason for a low score in this mode. Do not require requesting information already in the vignette.
Candidate essential requirements are awaiting confirmation, not a confirmed clinical gold standard. Apply their stated assumptions consistently. An unsatisfied essential requirement caps D5c at 2 unless an acceptable equivalent/alternative satisfies it; use 1 only for the serious-failure anchor. Do not require exact wording or hindsight of hidden diagnosis. Interpret each request against what was known when it could be made.

{"visible_record": {"initial_information_actually_supplied": "A 65-year-old man with ulcerative colitis treated with mesalamine developed a prolonged illness after a sore throat. For about five weeks he has had fever, night sweats, arthralgia and abdominal symptoms. An earlier admission found inflammatory and liver-test abnormalities, but colonoscopy did not show active colitis. Antibiotics and a short prednisone course did not resolve the illness. A low-level EBV DNA result and positive viral-capsid IgM/IgG had led to a working diagnosis of primary EBV infection.
He later developed palpable purpura on the flanks and upper thighs, purpura on the lower legs, transient scrotal pain, joint pain and leg oedema. Earlier urinalyses were normal; at the new admission urine has 2+ protein, 1+ blood and 5–10 red cells/high-power field, with protein:creatinine ratio 0.99. Creatinine is 0.72 mg/dL, albumin 2.6 g/dL and platelets 505000/microlitre. CT shows small-bowel thickening, surrounding inflammatory change and small-volume ascites. He is febrile but haemodynamically stable and mentally alert.
He lived in West Africa and Southeast Asia more than ten years ago, travelled to Florida seven months ago and cleans a neighbour’s chicken coop. A rapid P. falciparum antigen test is positive, but thick and thin blood smears on two days are negative. Biopsy findings and later response are not supplied.", "original_task": "Audience: a clinician. Use 200–280 words in English. Synthesise the main clinical problem, compare up to three useful explanations and reconcile the positive antigen, negative smears, earlier EBV interpretation and new urine findings. Separate observed facts, hypotheses and proposed actions. Do not invent measurements, negative findings, treatment responses or probabilities. Do not give a drug dose or a fixed treatment regimen. Give concise clinical justifications, not a private reasoning trace.", "audience": "Clinician", "task_mode": "written", "actual_dialogue_and_public_notes": [], "closing_public_assessment_note": {}, "final_answer_unchanged": "Observed facts: 65‑year‑old man with ulcerative colitis on mesalamine; five‑week febrile illness with night sweats, arthralgia, abdominal symptoms; prior admission showed inflammatory and liver‑test abnormalities, colonoscopy negative for active colitis; antibiotics and brief prednisone failed; low‑level EBV DNA, positive VCA IgM/IgG interpreted as primary EBV. New findings: palpable purpura on flanks, thighs, lower legs; transient scrotal pain; joint pain; leg oedema; urine 2+ protein, 1+ blood, 5‑10 RBC/HPF, protein:creatinine 0.99; creatinine 0.72 mg/dL, albumin 2.6 g/dL, platelets 505 000/µL; CT shows small‑bowel thickening, inflammatory change, small ascites; febrile, hemodynamically stable. Travel: West Africa, SE Asia >10 years ago; Florida 7 months ago; chicken‑coop exposure. Rapid P. falciparum antigen positive; thick/thin smears negative on two days.

Hypotheses: 1) EBV‑associated systemic illness with secondary vasculitis/renal involvement; 2) Acute malaria (false‑positive antigen or low‑level parasitaemia below smear detection) causing fever, thrombocytosis, bowel edema; 3) Henoch‑Schönlein purpura/IgA vasculitis triggered by infection (EBV or malaria) producing purpura, arthralgia, renal findings, bowel wall thickening.

Proposed actions: Repeat quantitative malaria PCR and thick smear daily for 3 days; obtain EBV quantitative PCR trend and heterophile test; urine microscopy for dysmorphic RBCs, urine protein electrophoresis; serum IgA, complement C3/C4, cryoglobulins; skin biopsy of purpura for IgA deposition; consider renal biopsy if proteinuria persists; monitor renal function, platelet trend, abdominal imaging for evolving bowel disease.", "deterministic_word_count": {"words": 216, "rule": "Body and heading text; Markdown/list markers removed; whitespace-separated; hyphenated forms count once; no extra tolerance.", "task_word_requirement": ["200–280 words"]}}, "rubric_item": {"id": "D5c", "name": "Targeted information seeking", "domain": "D5", "definition": "This sub-dimension assesses whether the model identifies and actively requests missing information needed for a defensible clinical assessment or decision. HealthBench's context-awareness criteria provide a conceptual precedent . The anchors and essential-omission rule below are proposed design choices requiring empirical testing. Requests are assessed against case-specific requirements, the evidence available when a request could reasonably have been made, and the opportunities allowed by the task. Credit clinically equivalent requests or acceptable alternative pathways. Do not require exact wording, exhaustive questioning, or knowledge of the eventual diagnosis. Case-specific requirements. Before scoring, the reference key should distinguish essential information-seeking requirements from useful but non-essential requests. An essential requirement is one whose omission materially compromises the assessment or decision required by the task. Its relevance must be justified by the presentation available at that point, not by hindsight from a hidden result or later outcome. The key should specify acceptable requests, alternatives, timing, and how the information can be obtained within the task constraints.", "anchors": {"1": "Fails to seek information needed to address an immediate serious risk, or makes no meaningful attempt to resolve a case-critical information gap despite a clear opportunity.", "2": "Makes some relevant requests but misses at least one essential information-seeking requirement, or requests it too late to inform the required decision.", "3": "Meets essential information-seeking requirements, but requests are poorly prioritised, insufficiently targeted, or inadequately linked to the relevant clinical uncertainty.", "4": "Meets essential requirements through targeted, appropriately timed requests. Avoids unnecessary information gathering."}, "context": "Essential-omission rule. Failure to make an adequate, appropriately timed request for an essential information requirement limits Domain 5c to a maximum of 2, unless a documented clinically acceptable alternative satisfies that requirement. Assign 1 where the serious-failure anchor applies. Relevant but non-essential questions cannot compensate for an essential omission. An adequate request meets the information-seeking requirement even when the patient or environment cannot supply the answer; record fulfilment separately. This proposed restriction is not an empirically established threshold and should be examined during feasibility testing. Requests and explanations. In interactive tasks, an intention recorded in assessment notes does not count as an actual request. Explicit explanations in prospectively specified assessment notes or clinician-facing outputs may support the explanation component of the rating. Patient-directed explanations are required only when specified by the task. Apply the same evidence rules to all models. A request's clinical relevance may be evident from context; do not require repetitive explanation of every question. Simulator and availability rules. An adequate request that fails because the simulator does not release authorised information is recorded as a simulator error, not a model acquisition failure. A request is not inadequate merely because the patient cannot answer or the information is unavailable. Record whether each essential request was made, whether it was fulfilled, and whether any failure was attributable to the model, environment, or an unresolved ambiguity. Applicability. Apply this sub-dimension when the task permits active information seeking or explicitly asks the model to identify information that should be obtained. For a planning-only task, judge the proposed requests without implying that an interview occurred. Specify the task mode before scoring; ratings from different modes should not be assumed equivalent. Rash evolution and symptom-timeline history are not explicitly requested, but the repeat urinalysis, renal-function trend and biopsy proposals provide an acceptable alternative pathway for R1.
